title: The Big Ideas in The Principles of Scientific Management
attribution: An original summary of the ideas in The Principles of Scientific Management by Frederick Winslow Taylor (1911). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher. If these ideas resonate, buy the full book.
summary:
Every meeting about productivity you have ever sat in is downstream of this thin, strange book. Taylor's argument is that management is not a matter of judgment, experience or personality but a subject with discoverable laws, and that the way to find them is to measure work with a stopwatch instead of asking anyone what they think.

He is also, by a wide margin, the most consequential management writer nobody defends. The methods went everywhere. The name became an insult.

# Soldiering, and why workers were right

Taylor's starting problem is that workers deliberately under-produce, a practice he calls soldiering. What makes his account interesting is that he does not treat it as laziness. He identifies the incentive precisely: when a worker's output rises, management historically responds by cutting the piece rate, so the worker ends up doing more for the same money. Producing at full capacity is therefore irrational, and every experienced hand knows it.

His conclusion, that the problem is the system rather than the character of the men, is the first genuinely modern management thought in the book. He also blames managers for the deeper failure: all the knowledge about how work is done sits in the heads of individual workers, is learned by watching whoever sat there before, and is nowhere written down. Nobody knows what a fair day's work actually is, so every negotiation is a bluff.

# Taking the knowledge out of the worker's head

The method follows. Break each job into elementary motions. Time each one. Discard the unnecessary ones and the slow ones. Reassemble the best sequence into a single prescribed procedure, write it down, and teach it.

The result, on Taylor's own accounts, was enormous: he reports pig-iron handling rising from twelve and a half tons a day to forty-seven, with the men paid substantially more. Modern researchers who have gone back to his records find the numbers dressed up, the anecdotes composited and the failures omitted. The magnitude of the underlying gain is still real; the reported figures are not evidence of anything.

What he is really doing is transferring knowledge from the worker to the organisation. That transfer is the whole story, and it explains both the productivity boom and the century of resentment. It makes the firm capable and the individual replaceable, in a single operation.

# The four principles, and the third one nobody quotes

Taylor states four duties for management. Develop a science for each element of work, replacing rule of thumb. Scientifically select and train the worker, rather than leaving them to pick it up. Cooperate with the workers to ensure the work is done according to the method. And divide the work so that management takes over the planning, which was formerly left to the workers.

The third is where the theory and the practice diverged fatally. Taylor genuinely believed the gains should be shared, that wages should rise with output, and that his system would end the conflict between labour and capital by making the pie large enough to stop arguing over. Firms adopted the stopwatch and the standardised procedure with enthusiasm, and adopted the wage increase and the cooperation rather less. The system that got implemented was his fourth principle without his third.

# The functional foreman, and the org chart nobody wanted

Buried in the middle is a structural proposal that failed completely and is worth knowing about because the failure is instructive. Taylor wanted to abolish the single foreman and replace him with eight specialists, each responsible for one dimension of a worker's job: one for speed, one for repairs, one for inspection, one for discipline, one for routing, and so on. A worker would answer to all eight.

The logic is consistent with everything else he believed. No individual can be expert at every aspect of a job, so splitting supervision by function should raise the quality of each decision. The practice was a disaster. Workers received contradictory instructions, nobody owned an outcome, and firms that tried it quietly reverted.

What went wrong is the thing his whole system is blind to. Coordination is itself work, and pushing it onto the person with the least authority does not eliminate the cost, it just moves it somewhere it cannot be measured. Every matrix organisation since has rediscovered this, usually about eighteen months after the reorganisation was announced.

# What it cost

The deficits are not subtle and Taylor half-states them himself, in language that makes modern readers wince: most famously his description of the ideal pig-iron handler as a man so stupid he more nearly resembles an ox. He assumes workers have nothing to contribute beyond compliance, which contradicts the observation he started from, that all the useful knowledge lived in their heads.

The deeper cost is the split between thinking and doing. Once planning belongs to a separate department, the person performing the work is structurally prevented from improving it, and the organisation loses the improvements they would have found. Later manufacturing systems built around continuous improvement from the line are, in effect, a correction of exactly this error: keeping Taylor's measurement and reversing his allocation of judgment.

# Where it still runs

The framework never disappeared; it migrated. Warehouse pick rates, call-centre handle times, delivery route optimisation and platform work of every kind are Taylorism with better instruments, and the stopwatch is now the device the worker is already holding.

It also migrated into knowledge work, where it fits worst. Measuring elementary motions works when the output is a moved ton of iron. It fails when the output is a decision, because the measurable proxies — tickets closed, lines written, calls handled — are gameable and only loosely connected to value. Every organisation that has ever ranked engineers by commit count has rediscovered soldiering, from the other end.

# The honest verdict

Taylor was right that work could be studied instead of guessed at, and that the alternative to measurement is not freedom but arbitrary authority based on whoever shouts. That is a real contribution and it survived him.

He was wrong that the people doing the work have nothing to contribute to how it is done, and that error was expensive enough to define the century of management theory that followed. Most of which can be read as an argument with a stopwatch.

learnings.text: Workers under-produce rationally rather than lazily: raising output historically triggered a cut in the piece rate, so full effort was punished.
Taylor's first modern insight is that the problem lies in the system rather than in the character of the workers.

The method is decomposition: break a job into elementary motions, time them, discard the unnecessary, then reassemble and teach the best sequence.

His reported productivity figures were dressed up and composited, though the underlying gains from method standardisation were genuine.
